solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: CIA scrambling to cover up as it's out of the continent

indicators.note: to scramble is to jumble or mix up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: The spy agency hurries to hush something up, since it came from another continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven letters of CIA and 'as it' are jumbled together; 'to cover up' only dresses the surface, suggesting a spy agency's cover-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that comes from Asia, the largest continent, is described by this adjective of origin.

clue.text: see 16dn.
On tour, rips out knob?

indicators.note: something put out of order or out of shape is disarranged, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone on a tour tears off a knob, with a smutty Private Eye wink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the phrase 'rips out', but it is the signal to rearrange the ten letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A knob is a rounded lump sticking out from a surface, which is exactly a bulging projection.

clue.text: One tabloid's topless sex hack

indicators.note: without a top means the uppermost, first letter is removed

blocks.note: the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, losing its first letter
'it' is a coy word for sex
a hack is a journalist, here the editor, ED

explanation.surface: A journalist at a red-top paper known for topless models and sex stories.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid once famous for topless Page 3 models, which makes 'topless' doubly apt. UN + IT + ED.
explanation.definitionFit: When several things become one, they are joined together into a single whole.

clue.text: Old queen's live sex show debuts

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: to live is to be, to exist
first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A former queen making her first appearance in a live sex show.
explanation.walkthrough: Good Queen Bess was the popular name for Elizabeth I of England.
explanation.definitionFit: This pet name for Elizabeth I names a monarch of long ago, a Tudor queen of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Where Trump likes to retreat, being beat up over race

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: a course is a race, as in a horse race run over a course

explanation.surface: Trump, beaten over the issue of race, retreats to his favourite bolthole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat up' looks like a phrase meaning assaulted, but 'up' turns the beating word backwards, and 'over' places it above the second part in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump famously spends much time playing golf at his own resorts, so his favourite retreat is a links.

clue.text: Initial coronavirus lockdown advice, with government initially holding out

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: the first lockdown message was to stay in at home

explanation.surface: Early pandemic lockdown advice, with the government at first holding back.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides at the end: 'holding out' looks like part of the government story.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold out is to endure or keep going, which is what lasting or persisting means.

clue.text: Scottish moneybags constructing bridges to carry old posh car

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: bridges span rivers; spans are bridges
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Wealthy Scots building bridges big enough to carry a vintage luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moneybags' suggests rich people, but it is literal: pouches for money. The posh car is a Rolls-Royce.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporran is the pouch worn at the front of a Scottish kilt, used as a purse for cash.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Good to be on top of wishy-washy liberal, having ditched presidential candidate, pet?

indicators.note: something wishy-washy is feeble and lacks firm shape, so these letters are loosened into a new order
to ditch is to throw away, so some letters are dropped
in a down entry, being on top of something means coming before it

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
Al Gore, the defeated US presidential candidate of 2000

explanation.surface: Is it good to beat a feeble liberal who has dropped their presidential candidate?
explanation.walkthrough: The candidate is Al Gore, beaten by George W. Bush in 2000. In a down entry, being 'on top of' puts the abbreviation for good first.
explanation.definitionFit: A gerbil is a small desert rodent commonly kept by children as a household pet.

clue.text: Scrutinize gold stuck on former royal toilet top

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Inspecting the gold fixed to a one-time royal's toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: DI is Diana, Princess of Wales, the former royal.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is an official examination of accounts, so to audit is to inspect closely and check.

clue.text: Some sucker, distraught, left – "Tess Daly's back!"

indicators.note: someone distraught is all shaken up, so these letters are thrown into disorder
the back of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A fan left in despair cries out that the TV presenter Tess Daly has returned.
explanation.walkthrough: Tess Daly hosts the BBC dance show Strictly Come Dancing. The eight letters of 'left' and 'Tess' are mixed, then the last of Daly is added.
explanation.definitionFit: This African insect feeds by sucking blood, so it is one example of a bloodsucker.

clue.text: (& 9ac./24dn.) Rueful thought of Cyclops during lockdown, as confessed in Pedantry Corner?

definitions.text: Rueful thought of Cyclops during lockdown, as confessed in Pedantry Corner?

blocks.clueFragment: Rueful thought of Cyclops during lockdown
blocks.note: surface reading: the setter, stuck indoors, regrets not leaving home
setter's reading: the stock self-mocking phrase of a pedant who admits to having no life

explanation.surface: The setter, confined at home in lockdown, wistfully confesses to fussy pedantic habits.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's letters page features nitpickers who often sign off admitting they lead sad lives; in lockdown the phrase takes on a literal sense too.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a self-deprecating admission of having too narrow a social life, typical of pedants.

clue.text: Constitution has race problem? That's Matt Hancock's province

indicators.note: a problem is something gone wrong, so these letters are in the wrong order and must be put right

blocks.note: one's constitution is one's physical condition

explanation.surface: A national constitution with a racial problem, set against a government minister's brief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constitution' looks political but means physical condition. Matt Hancock was the UK Health Secretary during the pandemic.
explanation.definitionFit: Hancock's ministerial portfolio covered the NHS and medical services, which is his department's area of responsibility.

clue.text: Brown needs balls and new plonker

blocks.note: balls are round, like two letter Os
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown needs courage and a fresh idiot by his side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' looks like the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, but it is the colour. Plonker is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A plonker is a foolish, clownish person, the same as a ridiculous joker or clown.

clue.text: (2dn.) An oath, e.g. "Fake!"

blocks.note: first meaning: a swear or rude expletive, the kind of short profanity bleeped on air
second meaning: literally a term with four characters, as this example has

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation suggests Trump's cry of 'Fake news!'; literally, 'fake' has four letters, and figuratively the phrase means a swear word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a rude expletive, since many common English swear words happen to be four characters long.

clue.text: Boiling tar oil and a gun that Trump would use against BLM protestors?

definitions.text: that Trump would use against BLM protestors?

indicators.note: boiling liquid churns and bubbles, so these letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters including the joining word

explanation.surface: Boiling tar, oil and guns: the weapons a president might turn on Black Lives Matter marchers.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'and' between the two pieces is part of the letters to be mixed, giving thirteen in all. BLM is Black Lives Matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump threatened to deploy this reserve military force, controlled by US states, against protests in American cities in 2020.

clue.text: Reckless Trumpean dismissing PM's constitution

indicators.note: to dismiss is to send away, so some letters are removed
something reckless is wild and careless, so these letters are rearranged without regard to order

explanation.surface: A reckless Trump-like figure tearing up the Prime Minister's constitution.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P and M from TRUMPEAN, leaving TRUEAN, then mix those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's constitution is their basic makeup or character, which is their essential temperament.

clue.text: Go away, rather coarsely protecting rear, to repel an attack

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: the vulgar dismissal, abbreviated with its initial

explanation.surface: Telling an attacker to clear off rudely while guarding one's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The coarse 'go away' is F-off; it wraps around END.
explanation.definitionFit: To ward off an assailant or blow is to keep it at a distance and resist it successfully.

clue.text: Dissolute, 'at it', he's no monk

indicators.note: dissolute means loose and dissipated, so these letters are loosened into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A loose-living man, always having sex, is plainly no monk.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a debauched man always 'at it' has no religious vocation, and an unbeliever would never be a monk.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk is devoted to God, so a nonbeliever who rejects any deity is the opposite of one.

clue.text: Old Tory leader in court – wiped out

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so the first letter is taken

blocks.note: CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A former Conservative leader in court, ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Tory leader' reads as an ex-party leader, but it splits into EX and the first letter of Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: A species that has been entirely eliminated no longer exists, having died out completely.

clue.text: Conservative and overtly leftist Labour sources, etc, surprisingly converge

indicators.note: a source is where something starts, so the first letters are taken
something surprising comes out unexpectedly, so these letters appear in an unexpected order

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Tories and openly left-wing Labour figures unexpectedly find common ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sources' looks like Labour insiders but asks for the first letters of the three words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: When people gather together at one place, they assemble or come together as a group.

clue.text: Prison made for Frank

blocks.note: to make is to do, so made is did

explanation.surface: A jail built for a man named Frank.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital F makes 'Frank' look like a name, but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means speaking honestly and openly, which is what an outspoken truthful person is.

clue.text: Classic tales of Ian Hislop backing Tory PM

indicators.note: to back is to move backwards, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: Hislop is the editor of Private Eye, ED

explanation.surface: Private Eye's editor supporting a Conservative Prime Minister, a classic tale indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like political support, but it turns ED round. Hislop edits Private Eye, where this puzzle appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's fourteenth-century work is a celebrated collection of a hundred stories told by Florentines escaping plague.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Trump's inauguration here – fake number!

indicators.note: an inauguration is a beginning, so the first letter is taken
a fake is a forgery, something made up, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A jibe about the crowd size claimed at Trump's inauguration being a made-up figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Trump's claims about the size of his inauguration crowd were widely called false, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Three is a cardinal numeral, the integer after two, and so an example of a number.

clue.text: Look like a dirty old man up wind

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading bottom to top, backwards

blocks.clueFragment: Look like a dirty old man
blocks.note: a lecherous look is a leer

explanation.surface: A lecherous old man ogling someone in a windy spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up wind' reads like 'upwind', but 'up' turns the leering word round and 'wind' is the definition, as in winding in a fishing line.
explanation.definitionFit: To reel in a line is to turn the spool and wind it around, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Four bollocks – about to make a big fuss

indicators.note: bollocks is British slang for nonsense, so the letters become a mess to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with four testicles might well cause a commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' looks like a noun counted by 'Four', but it is the slang word for rubbish, signalling a jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A furore is an outburst of public anger or excitement, a commotion or uproar.

clue.text: Like a nerd, you might say, left snapping selfies?

definitions.text: Like a nerd, you might say

indicators.note: to snap is to break apart, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A geek taking selfies, left on their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snapping' looks like taking photographs of selfies, but it breaks them up. 'You might say' admits the definition is an insult rather than a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerd is stereotyped as having no social life, so jokingly as dull and without vitality.
